title: Bronze statuette of a dog

altText: A small bronze statuette of a dog. The metal figure shows the animal's head, body, legs, and tail in a fixed pose.

context: A small bronze dog made in the Roman world in the 2nd to 3rd century CE. Dogs were familiar companions, guards, and working animals in Roman life, and they appear often in Roman art.

descriptions.k: This is a dog made of metal. It is very old. A Roman artist made it almost 2,000 years ago. Look at its head, its legs, and its tail. What do you think this dog likes to do?
descriptions.g12: A Roman artist made this small metal dog about 1,800 years ago. The metal is called bronze. Dogs lived with people in ancient Rome, just as they do today. Look at the dog's head, legs, and tail. What might the dog be listening to, smelling, or watching? Give it a name.
descriptions.g35: This little dog was cast in bronze, a metal made from copper mixed with tin, in the Roman Empire around the 2nd or 3rd century CE. Romans kept dogs as guards, helpers, and pets. The artist captured the animal's shape in metal that would last for centuries. Look at the pose and the details. What do they tell you about the dog's personality?
descriptions.g68: Bronze statuettes were popular in the Roman world, and animals were common subjects. This dog, dated to the 2nd–3rd century CE, shows how artists observed living animals and shaped metal to capture their character. Romans valued dogs as guardians and companions, and an image of a dog could have decorated a home or served another purpose we cannot confirm. Look at the proportions and posture. Which choices make the figure feel alive instead of generic?
descriptions.g910: This statuette demonstrates how a small bronze can carry a strong sense of character. Roman bronze workers often cast figures in metal, then refined the surface, and the success of the work depends on observation of the animal's posture and proportions. Dogs appear in Roman life as guardians, hunting helpers, and companions, so the figure may have had decorative, religious, or personal meaning that the record does not specify. Consider how the metal's solidity and shine shape the dog's presence.
descriptions.g1112: A bronze dog of the Roman Imperial period raises questions about how small figures function in cultural memory. Its naturalism, combined with the durable, reflective surface of bronze, creates a sense of presence in a very small form. Scholars note that animal images in Roman contexts could be decorative, votive, or tied to personal affection, but this record does not establish which applies here, so claims about its use remain provisional. Consider how scale, material, and observed behavior combine to make the dog seem familiar across nearly two thousand years.

teacherNote.context: A small bronze dog of the Roman Imperial period (2nd–3rd century CE). Bronze is an alloy mainly of copper and tin, and Romans produced many small bronze figures.
directions: Ask students to draw a pet or animal from three viewpoints, then discuss why a sculpture must work from every side.
Compare this bronze dog with a modern photograph of a dog: what does each show best?
Discuss why metal objects survive and what we can learn from small everyday objects.
